image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Diagrammatic grid / unit chart (waffle-style voter grid) with example district partitions.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiples**: one main 5×5 voter grid at the top and three example districting layouts below.  
   - Uses **grouping/partition overlays**: shaded outlines/regions indicate districts.  
   - Uses **color encoding** to distinguish party affiliation.  
   - Not a standard faceted statistical chart with axes; no stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Party affiliation (Blue party / Red party) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of voter dots (blue vs red); colored numeric labels |
| Individual voter / voter unit | Categorical/nominal (entity) | Repeated unit marks arranged in a 5×5 grid |
| Grid position / location in state grid | Ordinal/spatial arrangement | Position in rows and columns |
| District membership | Categorical/nominal | Grouping by shaded district regions/outlined areas in the example panels |
| Blue count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in blue box above each panel/example |
| Red count per example | Quantitative | Numeric label in red box above each panel/example |

This image shows three graph examples of how district maps are drawn can affect the outcome of an election. Each graph is a square and is made up of 25 blue and red dots that represent voters. There are three rows of blue dots on top and two rows of red dots on the bottom. In the first graph the dots are divided into columns representing voting districts. When the lines are drawn this way it is clearly biased towards the blue party because it makes all districts majority blue. I think the second graph is the most fair, the second graph draws the district lines in rows making every vote count. The third graph is extremely biased towards the red party because even though there are less red votes than blue, the way it is drawn makes the red party win the election. I wonder exactly how the government ensures that these maps are drawn fairly.

1) I notice that in the graphs above, 2/3 voting districts are drawn in a way so that the vote does not ultimately reflect the opinions of the population. Even though most voters support blue, the graph on the left where blue wins is not fair because the vote ended up 5-0, which is not representative of the population. I noticed that in the graph on the far right, red won despite most people in the population supporting blue. It also has the most distorted voting districts.

2) I wonder how gerrymandering has been allowed to this extent. I also wonder if any initiatives or legislation is in place to restrict the degree as to how politicians can distort districts when drawing them.

3) This relates to me and my community because we live in the United States and our voting district is subject to change when the district maps are redrawn. I don't doubt that gerrymandering has occurred in my area, and when I become old enough to vote my voting patterns and the voting patterns of those around me may play a role in how the voting districts are drawn.

4) In the graph, it shows several ways voting districts would be organized in a hypothetical area in a perfect grid. A catchy headline for this graph could be "Take a gander when politicians gerrymander!"

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice first off that the ratio stays 60% blue and 40% red no matter how you slice it. I also notice that once they start dividing it into the examples of districts, some of the dots are highlighted in red while others are highlighted in blue. From that i conclude that whichever color they are highlighted is the party which majority of the votes will go to. I also notice that as there are more examples the gap between districts red and districts blue gets smaller. It starts off at 5 blue 0 red and finishes with 2 blue and 3 red. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder how this strategy is used in real life. Say there is a state that is 60% blue party and 40% red party, yet the state is a 'red state' based on election results. Who divides districts? Is it meant to sway the states electoral votes one way or another? 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community at the moment more than me personally for the sole reason that I cannot vote yet given that I am not 18. But, this relates to my community and my neighbors views representation. Our districts vote counts, and how my neighbors and parents vote help decide how the district votes. 
Headline?
"Statistics, statistics...Do they truly matter?"

Is there ever a true way to be completely "fair" so that each party feels validated? Should the majority always win--is it really more/less fair to split districts this way? This relates to my community as I am a citizen of the Untied states, following these two political parties. Since I'll be of voting age soon, this will also affect me more directly then. A headline could be: "The People or the Boundaries--Who has the Say?"

In the  graph on the left and the graph on the right, there are checkers that are red in blue areas and vice versa. I wonder if this is how gerrymandering works. If so, how does it get passed without anyone saying anything? I'm also wondering how complicated it gets when a state does not have a perfect grid. 

This affects me and my community because the government can change the national and state congressional districts, which could change how certain ones vote in an election.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s infographics shows how states can redistrict their voters which can change the balance of power in state and federal legislative bodies.  These are very timely infographic.  In the past two days, the New York Times has published front page articles on redistricting in Texas and California.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these infographics and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Dec. 17 with moderation on Wednesday, Jan. 5.  The topic – to be determined.  Keep noticing and wondering.  See you in 2022.

comments.raw_comment:
1. Immediately, it is clear that all four diagrams have the same number of "voters." Each voter is put in a specific district for congressional and state legislatures. However, despite their being a larger number of "blue" voters, the "red" voters are able to be redistricted in a manner that benefits them and disadvantages the more heavily supported "blue" party.
2. I wonder when the United States will nationally standardize a specific system to redistrict appropriately. For example, some states hire nonpartisan organizations to redistrict their respective populations. However, many states continue to unfairly redistrict the populace.
3. This graph relates to my community and I because redistricting plays a vital role in the state. New York's voters are predominantly part of the Democratic Party; however, if the state were gerrymandered in favor of the Republican Party, it is possible that the state would vote in more republicans in legislative positions.
4. The graph depicts three examples of a single district being gerrymandered. It illustrates an equal way, with the majority having control, and two unequal methods, in which one party monopolizes control over the other. Overall, the graph demonstrates a major issue present in the United States' government. A catchy headline could be "The Flaw That Can Change Elections: Gerrymandering"

comments.raw_comment:
In the population of 25 voters, 60% vote Blue and 40% vote Red. 
Of 3 examples for voter districts, 2 of them stand out as non-representative of the voter population.
The center example has voting districts separated strictly by party; no districts have any party variety. 
The graph on the right shows districts being chosen in a manner that sort of 'hand picks' the Red party to be the majority rule. The Blue to Red ratio of each district fails to represent the ratio of the voter population.
The left example shows each district with a 3:2 Blue to Red ratio, which IS representative of this ratio in the voter population. 

I wonder if there's an accurate way of dividing the voters into districts, with minimal corrupt interference. 
The graph on the right, for example, appears to be the least uniform and most varied, but seems to be divided in a way that intentionally pushes the ball toward the Red party, despite having less voters (this could be Gerrymandering).
But if you apply that logic, how is it possible to divide voters without leaning more toward one party? By this logic, would the other two be just as manipulative?

This relates to my community because the American voting system seems skewed, and muffles the voice of the people who vote. How often do you see a candidate lose popular vote but win the electoral votes (2000 and 2016)? How often is either party accused of Gerrymandering? Very.

The graph shows that voter districts can be divided to help one given party win.

comments.raw_comment: Gerrymandering is an incredibly interesting concept in politics. Manipulating the boundaries of an electoral constituency to favor one party is a practice that has been done since the early 19th century. In this graph, I notice who has the majority (blue) and who is in the minority (red). In an ideal and fair election, the goal would be to have both parties represented in each district. I would interpret the first of the three examples as unfair and unequal, because the blue party is the majority in all 5 districts. The second and third graphs, although not equal, are more fair. Within the five districts, they have both parties represented as a majority which is important. This is important because it allows for a more balanced representation of constituents. In a more personal context, this is important because if I were to vote for red party in the all blue party dominated districts, my vote would get lost and lose its value, as well as my faith in a fair voting system

What do I notice?

I notice that blue voters have the majority of 60% percent of votes in the graph, while red voters have the minority with 40%. I also notice that the graph is trying to show what potential voting districts would look like, either isolating voters of the same party with each other or mixing both blue and red voters together.

What do I wonder?

I wonder which one of those graphs is the most fair for drawing voting districts. Is it better to have voters of different parties influence each other? Or should we have like-minded people be in the same district? Who gets to decide how these voting lines will be drawn?

How does this relate to me and my community?

This relates to me and everyone’s community because the way these districts are drawn will affect which party controls our state’s government. We need to find a way to draw these districts where voices of both parties are heard.

Catchy headline: Red or Blue- Which District Are You?

If voting district lines are drawn unfairly, giving the minority an advantage, then a majority of people will be unhappy with who ends up elected.
